<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

  .arxiv-html-header { display: contents; }

  /* The paper controls' icons are blocks, so they sit centred (the pinned JS shows the theme
     icon by making its span a block). */
  .arxiv-html-site-chrome .ds-site-header-tools svg { display: block; width: 18px; height: 18px; flex-shrink: 0; fill: currentColor; }
  /* ar5iv dims every image in dark mode and puts it on a white wash, for paper figures;
     arXiv's own render as they are (the logo on the bar, the funder logos on their white
     chips). Important: ar5iv's dark rules are unlayered, as specific as
     :root:not([data-theme]) img:not(.ltx_no_dark_filter). */
  :is(.ds-site-header, .ds-site-footer) img { filter: none !important; }
  .ds-site-header img { background-color: transparent !important; }

  /* Wide (the theme's 1280px): the theme lays the body out as a grid whose full-width top rows
     were the band's and its sticky reader bar's. The band takes the first and scrolls away; the
     header, the paper's bar (no site navigation, the paper's controls), takes the second and
     stays in view, the one sticky bar, with the anchor clearance that requires (DESIGN-POLICIES).
     The controls show their names. */
  @media (min-width: 1280px) {
    html { scroll-padding-top: 80px; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome { display: contents; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome > #ds-announcement { grid-area: announce; }

    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-icon { display: none; }
  }
  /* Narrow: the header scrolls away, and the controls show icons (names kept for screen
     readers; Why HTML? goes). The theme's contents panel is fixed below where its old sticky
     bar was, and hidden only once the reader has closed it, so until then it is an invisible box
     over the header and the paper: it shows only while open, under the chrome, in its place in
     the page. The paper's footer (build logs, reporting instructions) keeps the text's side
     inset; the theme gives it none, so it met the screen edges. */
  @media (max-width: 1279px) {
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-wide { display: none; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-label { position: absolute; width: 1px; height: 1px; overflow: hidden; clip: rect(0 0 0 0); white-space: nowrap; }
    html:not([data-toc-display="block"]) .ltx_page_navbar { display: none; }
    .ltx_page_navbar { position: absolute; top: auto; }

<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_paragraph"><a href="#A10.SS7.SSS0.Px1" title="In J.7 Multi-source distractors and MCQ verification ‣ Appendix J Prompts Used in Data Construction ‣ ZoomGain: Mining Global-to-Zoom Perception Gaps for Fine-Grained Visual Supervision" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">FULL_DISTRACTOR_CLUSTERING</span>.</span></a></li>
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_paragraph"><a href="#A10.SS7.SSS0.Px2" title="In J.7 Multi-source distractors and MCQ verification ‣ Appendix J Prompts Used in Data Construction ‣ ZoomGain: Mining Global-to-Zoom Perception Gaps for Fine-Grained Visual Supervision" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">BLIND_DISTRACTOR_CLUSTERING</span>.</span></a></li>
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_paragraph"><a href="#A10.SS7.SSS0.Px3" title="In J.7 Multi-source distractors and MCQ verification ‣ Appendix J Prompts Used in Data Construction ‣ ZoomGain: Mining Global-to-Zoom Perception Gaps for Fine-Grained Visual Supervision" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">VLM_DISTRACTOR_GENERATOR</span>.</span></a></li>

<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line" lang="en">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">ZoomGain: Mining Global-to-Zoom Perception Gaps for Fine-Grained Visual Supervision</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">
<span id="id1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_align_middle">
<span class="ltx_tbody">
<span id="id1.1" class="ltx_tr">
<span id="id1.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center" style="padding-bottom: 3.0pt;">Haozhan Shen<sup id="id1.1.1.1" class="ltx_sup"><span id="id1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">1,2∗</span></sup> Liangbo He<sup id="id1.1.1.2" class="ltx_sup">1</sup> Jun Lan<sup id="id1.1.1.3" class="ltx_sup"><span id="id1.1.1.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">1†</span></sup> Huijia Zhu<sup id="id1.1.1.4" class="ltx_sup">1</sup></span></span>
<span id="id1.2" class="ltx_tr">
<span id="id1.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center">Weiqiang Wang<sup id="id1.2.1.1" class="ltx_sup">1</sup> Tiancheng Zhao<sup id="id1.2.1.2" class="ltx_sup"><span id="id1.2.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">3,4†</span></sup> Jianwei Yin<sup id="id1.2.1.3" class="ltx_sup">1</sup></span></span>
</span>
</span>
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>
<table id="id2" class="ltx_tabular ltx_align_middle">
<tbody class="ltx_tbody">
<tr id="id2.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="id2.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center" style="padding-bottom: 2.0pt;"><sup id="id2.1.1.1" class="ltx_sup">1</sup>Ant Group <sup id="id2.1.1.2" class="ltx_sup">2</sup>Zhejiang University</td></tr>
<tr id="id2.2" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="id2.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center"><sup id="id2.2.1.1" class="ltx_sup">3</sup>Om AI Research <sup id="id2.2.1.2" class="ltx_sup">4</sup>Binjiang Institute of Zhejiang University</td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Fine-grained visual perception requires Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to locate and interpret subtle evidence within complex scenes.
Constructing supervision for this ability is challenging:
questions must have correct, unambiguous answers that depend on actual fine-grained visual details rather than coarse cues or language priors.
Verifying these properties makes manual annotation labor-intensive and automatic generation difficult for models that themselves struggle with fine-grained perception.
Yet the same models can often recognize such details once the region is zoomed in.
We exploit this global-to-zoom perception gap and introduce <span id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">ZoomGain</span>,
a data construction pipeline that constructs questions about the full image
from visual information <span id="abstract1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">gain</span>ed <span id="abstract1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">only</span> by <span id="abstract1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">zoom</span>ing in.
It verifies each answer on the zoomed view with multiple models,
ensures that each question remains unambiguous in the full image and cannot be answered from language priors,
and specifically generates high-quality distractors for multiple-choice questions.
With this pipeline and human-only screening (no manual QA editing),
we build ZoomGainBench, a 1,000-question bilingual benchmark on which the best of 28 VLMs achieves only 61.08.
Failure analysis reveals that models favor a particular type of distractor
when answering multiple-choice questions incorrectly.
Beyond evaluation, training on just 9K ZoomGain samples
substantially improves the visual perception capabilities of our 4B/9B models,
enabling them to outperform several hundred-billion-parameter models across various perception benchmarks.
The trained 9B model achieves SoTA performance on several benchmarks, such as 90.25 on HR-Bench 4K.
These results establish global-to-zoom perception gaps as a practical basis for scaling fine-grained visual supervision for both evaluation and training.
Our code is available at <a href="https://github.com/inclusionAI/ZoomGain" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">https://github.com/inclusionAI/ZoomGain</a>.</p>
  
</div><span id="footnotex1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnotetext"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_type">footnotetext: </span><sup id="footnotex1.1" class="ltx_sup">*</sup>Work done during an internship at Ant Group.
<br class="ltx_break"><sup id="footnotex1.2" class="ltx_sup"><math id="footnotex1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\dagger" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>†</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\dagger</annotation></semantics></math></sup>Corresponding authors: Jun Lan (<a href="mailto:yelan.lj@antgroup.com" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">yelan.lj@antgroup.com</a>) and Tiancheng Zhao (<a href="mailto:tianchez@zju-bj.com" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">tianchez@zju-bj.com</a>).</span></span></span>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<figure id="S1.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2611.14076v1/zoomgain_overview_v8.png" id="S1.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/317;" width="476" height="317" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span><span id="S1.F1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">ZoomGain: turning global-to-zoom perception gaps into fine-grained visual supervision.</span>
(a) The runner’s shoe color is unclear in the global view but discernible in the zoomed view;
ZoomGain asks about such details in the full image,
using a global referring expression to identify the target.
The paired views <math id="S1.F1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V_{g}^{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>V</mi><mi>g</mi><mi>i</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V_{g}^{i}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S1.F1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V_{z}^{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>V</mi><mi>z</mi><mi>i</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V_{z}^{i}</annotation></semantics></math>, and the referring <math id="S1.F1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>e</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> are defined in Section <a href="#S3.SS2" title="3.2 Global-to-Zoom Evidence and QA Construction ‣ 3 ZoomGain Data Construction Pipeline ‣ ZoomGain: Mining Global-to-Zoom Perception Gaps for Fine-Grained Visual Supervision" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a>.
(b) ZoomGainBench, obtained by human screening without QA editing, challenges all 28 evaluated VLMs
(c) RLVR on 9K training QA pairs improves Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.5-9B
over their base models and ZwZ-trained counterparts (ICML’26 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wei et al. (2026)</a></cite>).
</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Fine-grained visual perception is essential in many practical applications,
from detecting small vehicles in aerial imagery <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xia et al. (2018)</a></cite> and
identifying subtle defects in industrial inspection <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bergmann et al. (2019)</a></cite>
to reading product labels for people with visual impairments <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gurari et al. (2018)</a></cite>.
Addressing such tasks with Vision-Language Models (VLMs) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Team (2026)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bai et al. (2025)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhu et al. (2025)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al. (2023)</a></cite> requires locating and interpreting
small details that are easily overlooked in the full image.
To develop and benchmark such fine-grained capabilities, high-quality supervision is essential:
answers must be correct and unambiguous,
and questions must genuinely require fine-grained visual evidence.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Constructing such supervision at scale is challenging.
Manual annotation is labor-intensive,
as annotators must inspect small regions and verify each of these properties.
Automatic generation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al. (2025a)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wei et al. (2026)</a></cite> faces a related difficulty:
the models used to generate questions may themselves struggle to perceive the relevant details in the full image.
As a result, they may produce incorrect answers, ambiguous references, or questions that do not actually require fine-grained perception.
Motivated by this, the key challenge is to obtain reliable supervision on visual details that models fail to perceive in full scenes.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Zooming in has long been used to recover such details,
either at inference time through visual search <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu and Xie (2023)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lai et al. (2025)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shen et al. (2025)</a></cite>
and agentic VLMs with cropping tools <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zheng et al. (2026)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hong et al. (2026)</a></cite>,
or during training through region-to-image distillation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wei et al. (2026)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yuan et al. (2026)</a></cite>,
since details a model fails to resolve in the full image often become recognizable
once the region is zoomed in.
We specifically use this global-to-zoom perception gap to construct the supervision itself
(Fig. <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ ZoomGain: Mining Global-to-Zoom Perception Gaps for Fine-Grained Visual Supervision" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> (a)):
contrasting the two views locates details that are hard to perceive in the full image.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Based on this idea, we introduce <span id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">ZoomGain</span>, an automated data construction pipeline
that converts visual information, which are <span id="S1.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">gain</span>ed <em id="S1.p4.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">only</em> by <span id="S1.p4.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">zoom</span>ing,
into challenging questions about the full image (<span id="S1.p4.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Contribution #1</span>).
ZoomGain (1) builds questions exclusively from details described in the zoomed view
but unclear or absent in the full-image description, so that answering requires the fine detail itself;
(2) keeps an answer only when multiple models agree on it in the zoomed view,
and discards questions with ambiguous full-image references or answerable without images;
and (3) generates various multiple-choice distractors that could mislead the queried VLMs.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Using ZoomGain, we curate <span id="S1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">ZoomGainBench</span>, a bilingual benchmark of 1,000 questions
on attribute recognition, counting, and OCR, whose questions and answers are entirely model-authored:
two human reviewers only accept/reject candidates (<span id="S1.p5.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Contribution #2</span>).
Among 28 evaluated VLMs, the best model, GPT-5.6-Sol, scores only 61.08,
and only five exceed 50 (Fig. <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ ZoomGain: Mining Global-to-Zoom Perception Gaps for Fine-Grained Visual Supervision" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>(b)).
Error analysis further reveals that incorrect choices concentrate on distractors
mined from full-image mispredictions during construction (Sec. <a href="#S3.SS3" title="3.3 Quality Verification and Multi-Source Distractors ‣ 3 ZoomGain Data Construction Pipeline ‣ ZoomGain: Mining Global-to-Zoom Perception Gaps for Fine-Grained Visual Supervision" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.3</span></a>).
This indicates that when details are unresolved,
models tend to fill the information gap with similar scene-plausible guesses,
suggesting that the global-to-zoom perception gap is a common weakness across current VLMs,
rather than an issue to specific models.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Beyond evaluation, ZoomGain data also serves as effective training supervision (<span id="S1.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Contribution #3</span>).
With identical source images and training settings,
we train Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.5-9B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Team (2026)</a></cite> on 9K ZoomGain and ZwZ (ICML’26 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wei et al. (2026)</a></cite>) QA pairs.
ZoomGain-trained models consistently outperform ZwZ across all 14 evaluated benchmarks (Fig. <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ ZoomGain: Mining Global-to-Zoom Perception Gaps for Fine-Grained Visual Supervision" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>(c)).
The gains extend beyond fine-grained perception to general perception
and difficult perception-and-reasoning tasks,
e.g., 11.01 points boost on O3-Bench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al. (2026a)</a></cite> for the 9B model.
Notably, our fine-tuned 9B model is on par with GLM-5.3-Flash <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">GLM-5-Team et al. (2026)</a></cite> and 4B model surpasses Qwen3.5-122B-A10B.
Ablations show that removing either incremental evidence or multi-source distractors
substantially reduces these gains,
confirming that both designs rooted in the global-to-zoom perception gap are essential.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Related Work</h2>

<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Fine-grained perception benchmarks.</h4>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A variety of benchmarks specifically evaluate fine-grained perception in high-resolution images,
including <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu and Xie (2023)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al. (2025b)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al. (2024)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al. (2025a)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gavrikov et al. (2026)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lai et al. (2025)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al. (2026b)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wei et al. (2026)</a></cite>;
O3-Bench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al. (2026a)</a></cite> further requires multi-step reasoning beyond perception.
However, questions in these benchmarks are typically annotated manually or generated by models with extensive manual editing (Table <a href="#S4.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ Training Data Selection and Matching. ‣ 4 Implementation Details and Data Preparation ‣ ZoomGain: Mining Global-to-Zoom Perception Gaps for Fine-Grained Visual Supervision" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>), making scalable cruation costly.
Moreover, existing benchmarks rarely filter out language-prior shortcuts <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cadene et al. (2019)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al. (2024)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yue et al. (2025)</a></cite>
or design targeted distractors. In contrast, ZoomGain fully automates QA authoring with zoom-view verification,
blind shortcut filtering, and distractor mining from model errors.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Improving fine-grained perception.</h4>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Zooming has been widely adopted to enhance fine-grained perception,
either at inference time via visual search <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu and Xie (2023)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shen et al. (2025)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lai et al. (2025)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al. (2026a)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al. ()</a></cite>
and agentic cropping tools <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zheng et al. (2026)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hong et al. (2026)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Su et al. (2026)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al. (2025)</a></cite>,
or during training through zoomed-to-global distillation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wei et al. (2026)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yuan et al. (2026)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al. (2026b)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al. (2026a)</a></cite>.
Unlike prior works that focus on inference procedures or training objectives,
ZoomGain targets data construction itself:
it leverages the global-to-zoom perception gap to identify what to ask (strictly on zoom-revealed details)
and reliably verify ground truth, making it complementary to existing approaches.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>ZoomGain Data Construction Pipeline</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">ZoomGain exploits the perception gap between global and zoomed-in views:
fine-grained details that are difficult to discern in the full image
may become clear once the target region is zoomed in.
As illustrated in Figure <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3 ZoomGain Data Construction Pipeline ‣ ZoomGain: Mining Global-to-Zoom Perception Gaps for Fine-Grained Visual Supervision" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>,
ZoomGain first discovers and grounds target anchors (Sec. <a href="#S3.SS1" title="3.1 Anchor Discovery and Grounding ‣ 3 ZoomGain Data Construction Pipeline ‣ ZoomGain: Mining Global-to-Zoom Perception Gaps for Fine-Grained Visual Supervision" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a>),
then constructs questions and answers from details newly revealed by zooming (Sec. <a href="#S3.SS2" title="3.2 Global-to-Zoom Evidence and QA Construction ‣ 3 ZoomGain Data Construction Pipeline ‣ ZoomGain: Mining Global-to-Zoom Perception Gaps for Fine-Grained Visual Supervision" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a>),
and finally verifies answer reliability and visual dependence
and builds multi-source distractors that capture plausible model errors (Sec.n <a href="#S3.SS3" title="3.3 Quality Verification and Multi-Source Distractors ‣ 3 ZoomGain Data Construction Pipeline ‣ ZoomGain: Mining Global-to-Zoom Perception Gaps for Fine-Grained Visual Supervision" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.3</span></a>).
The complete algorithm and additional implementation details are provided in
Appendix <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Complete Algorithm and Additional Implementation Details ‣ ZoomGain: Mining Global-to-Zoom Perception Gaps for Fine-Grained Visual Supervision" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F2" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2611.14076v1/zoomgain_pipeline_v5.png" id="S3.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/366;" width="476" height="366" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span><span id="S3.F2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Overview of ZoomGain.</span>
(a) Discover anchors and obtain consensus regions through independent grounding.
(b) Mine global-to-zoom incremental evidence from paired views to construct questions and reference answers.
(c) Verify answers and visual dependence, then assemble and recheck
multiple-choice questions with multi-source distractors.</figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Anchor Discovery and Grounding</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Given an input image, denoted as the global view <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V_{g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>g</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V_{g}</annotation></semantics></math>,
we first use a VLM to generate a global scene caption <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>g</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{g}</annotation></semantics></math>.
A text-only LLM then takes <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>g</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{g}</annotation></semantics></math> as its sole input
and proposes a set of candidate anchors.
Each anchor <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math> is represented by a referring expression <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>e</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>
that describes the target’s appearance, spatial location, or relations to other objects.
To ensure that <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>e</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> can identify a localizable instance unambiguously in the full image,
three VLMs independently ground <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>e</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> in <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V_{g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>g</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V_{g}</annotation></semantics></math>.
We retain <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>e</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> only if each model returns exactly one valid bounding box,
since a missing box or multiple boxes indicate that the referent cannot be found or may be ambiguous,
and all pairwise box IoUs are at least <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.5</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.5</annotation></semantics></math>,
which provides cross-model evidence that <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>e</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> refers to a consistent region.
For each retained anchor, we take the coordinate-wise median of the predicted boxes,
expand the resulting region to include more surrounding context,
yielding the crop box <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>, and crop <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V_{g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>g</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V_{g}</annotation></semantics></math> using <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> to obtain a zoomed view <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V_{z}^{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>V</mi><mi>z</mi><mi>i</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V_{z}^{i}</annotation></semantics></math>.
The quadruples <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(V_{g},V_{z}^{i},b_{i},e_{i})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>g</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>V</mi><mi>z</mi><mi>i</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>e</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(V_{g},V_{z}^{i},b_{i},e_{i})</annotation></semantics></math>
serve as inputs to the subsequent question construction stage.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Global-to-Zoom Evidence and QA Construction</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For each retained anchor <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>, we use a strong VLM <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M_{\mathrm{cap}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>cap</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M_{\mathrm{cap}}</annotation></semantics></math>
to describe the target region from both views.
Specifically, we draw a red bounding box at <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> in <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V_{g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>g</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V_{g}</annotation></semantics></math>
to obtain an annotated global view <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V_{g}^{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>V</mi><mi>g</mi><mi>i</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V_{g}^{i}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Figure <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ ZoomGain: Mining Global-to-Zoom Perception Gaps for Fine-Grained Visual Supervision" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>(a) illustrates the paired views <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(V_{g}^{i},V_{z}^{i})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>V</mi><mi>g</mi><mi>i</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>V</mi><mi>z</mi><mi>i</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(V_{g}^{i},V_{z}^{i})</annotation></semantics></math>.
We feed <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V_{g}^{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>V</mi><mi>g</mi><mi>i</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V_{g}^{i}</annotation></semantics></math> into <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M_{\mathrm{cap}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>cap</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M_{\mathrm{cap}}</annotation></semantics></math> and prompt it to describe
only the contents of the red box in as much detail as possible,
yielding the global-view caption <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{g}^{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>C</mi><mi>g</mi><mi>i</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{g}^{i}</annotation></semantics></math>.
In a separate, independent call,
we provide the zoomed view <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V_{z}^{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>V</mi><mi>z</mi><mi>i</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V_{z}^{i}</annotation></semantics></math> and request a detailed caption <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{z}^{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>C</mi><mi>z</mi><mi>i</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{z}^{i}</annotation></semantics></math>.
This produces two descriptions of the same region <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> at different viewing scales.
We then use an LLM to compare <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{g}^{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>C</mi><mi>g</mi><mi>i</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{g}^{i}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{z}^{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>C</mi><mi>z</mi><mi>i</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{z}^{i}</annotation></semantics></math>,
extracting details that are explicitly described in <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{z}^{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>C</mi><mi>z</mi><mi>i</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{z}^{i}</annotation></semantics></math>
but remain unclear or unmentioned in <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{g}^{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>C</mi><mi>g</mi><mi>i</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{g}^{i}</annotation></semantics></math>.
These details form a candidate fact set <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>.
For example, in Figure <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3 ZoomGain Data Construction Pipeline ‣ ZoomGain: Mining Global-to-Zoom Perception Gaps for Fine-Grained Visual Supervision" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>(b),
the runner’s shoe color is unclear in the global-view caption
but identified as red in the zoomed-view caption,
so it becomes a candidate fact in <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m18" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We generate three types of questions:
attribute recognition, text recognition (OCR), and counting.
An LLM selects one fact from <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> that supports a definite answer
and generates a local question <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q_{\mathrm{local}}^{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>q</mi><mi>local</mi><mi>i</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q_{\mathrm{local}}^{i}</annotation></semantics></math>
and a reference answer <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> based on this fact.
The local question is phrased for the zoomed view
with a simple reference such as “the runner”,
without specifying the target’s location in the full image.
The LLM then replaces this reference with the global referring expression <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>e</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>
and adjusts the wording to produce a global-view question <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q_{\mathrm{global}}^{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>q</mi><mi>global</mi><mi>i</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q_{\mathrm{global}}^{i}</annotation></semantics></math>,
keeping the queried detail and reference answer unchanged,
so that questions about details revealed by zooming
clearly identify the intended target in the full image.
For example, “What color are the runner’s shoe uppers?”
becomes “What color are the shoe uppers of
the dark-shirted runner on the right yellow line?”
Appendix <a href="#A8" title="Appendix H Global-to-Zoom Evidence and QA Construction Examples ‣ ZoomGain: Mining Global-to-Zoom Perception Gaps for Fine-Grained Visual Supervision" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">H</span></a> illustrates this construction process
with attribute, counting, and OCR examples.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Quality Verification and Multi-Source Distractors</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We verify each candidate QA pair in two ways.
(1) For <em id="S3.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">crop-based verification</em>, we provide several VLMs
with <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q_{\mathrm{local}}^{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>q</mi><mi>local</mi><mi>i</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q_{\mathrm{local}}^{i}</annotation></semantics></math> and the zoomed view <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V_{z}^{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>V</mi><mi>z</mi><mi>i</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V_{z}^{i}</annotation></semantics></math>,
and sample multiple answers from each model.
We retain the QA pair only if all models meet a predefined accuracy threshold on their sampled answers.
Checking agreement among multiple models answering based on the zoomed-view helps ensure answer correctness,
thereby avoiding sole reliance on a single model’s caption for answer annotation, which may contain hallucinations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rohrbach et al. (2018)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al. (2023)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jing et al. (2024)</a></cite>.
(2) For <em id="S3.SS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">blind verification</em>, models are asked to answer <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q_{\mathrm{global}}^{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>q</mi><mi>global</mi><mi>i</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q_{\mathrm{global}}^{i}</annotation></semantics></math> without an image.
We discard a QA if all blind models exceed a prescribed correct-answer threshold.
This step effectively filters out questions that can be answered through language priors alone rather than actual image content <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cadene et al. (2019)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al. (2024)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yue et al. (2025)</a></cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For verified QA pairs suited to multiple-choice evaluation,
we construct distractors from three complementary sources.
(1) <em id="S3.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Visual evidence</em> supplies plausible alternatives from image content,
such as the neon-green shoes of another runner in Figure <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3 ZoomGain Data Construction Pipeline ‣ ZoomGain: Mining Global-to-Zoom Perception Gaps for Fine-Grained Visual Supervision" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>(c),
which can expose errors in target selection or attribute binding.
(2) <em id="S3.SS3.p2.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Blind guesses</em> provide incorrect answers produced without the image,
capturing language priors.
(3) <em id="S3.SS3.p2.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Global-view errors</em> provide incorrect answers produced from the full image,
capturing confusions when local details are difficult to discern.
We remove candidates equivalent to the reference answer or also valid for the question,
merge semantically redundant candidates,
and normalize their wording to form distinct answer options.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We combine the reference answer with the selected distractors
and recheck the resulting MCQ using the zoomed view.
This final check tests whether the reference answer remains reliably distinguishable
after competing options are introduced.
If the per-model agreement thresholds are not met,
we replace or remove problematic distractors.
OCR and counting questions retain an open-ended format
and bypass distractor construction and MCQ rechecking.
Appendix <a href="#A9" title="Appendix I Quality Verification Examples ‣ ZoomGain: Mining Global-to-Zoom Perception Gaps for Fine-Grained Visual Supervision" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">I</span></a> provides examples of candidate QA pairs
rejected by crop-based and blind verification.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Implementation Details and Data Preparation</h2>

<section id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Model Roles and Verification Settings.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We use Qwen3.5-397B-A17B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Team (2026)</a></cite> as <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M_{\mathrm{cap}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>cap</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M_{\mathrm{cap}}</annotation></semantics></math>
and the initial global scene captioner.
GLM-5.2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">GLM-5-Team et al. (2026)</a></cite> performs incremental fact extraction and QA generation.
Global-view error distractors are mined from incorrect answers produced by
Qwen3.5-397B-A17B, Qwen3-VL-235B-A22B-Instruct <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bai et al. (2025)</a></cite>,
and Kimi-K2.6 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Team et al. (2026b)</a></cite>
to the global question on the full image,
with 10 answers sampled per model (30 in total).
All verification stages likewise sample 10 answers per model and apply per-model accuracy thresholds.
Complete model assignments, verification thresholds, and distractor repair settings are provided in
Appendix <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Construction Settings ‣ ZoomGain: Mining Global-to-Zoom Perception Gaps for Fine-Grained Visual Supervision" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Data Generation and Benchmark Curation.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We randomly sample 12K images from ZwZ <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wei et al. (2026)</a></cite>,
which collects high-resolution images from several sources <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kirillov et al. (2023)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chuang et al. (2025)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al. (2022)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Changpinyo et al. (2021)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Krishna et al. (2017)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schuhmann et al. (2022)</a></cite>,
and generate a pool of 23,610 QA pairs with ZoomGain.
GLM-5.2 jointly generates Chinese and English versions of both the local and global questions,
and the two language versions of a question are counted as one QA pair.
From this pool, two human reviewers select 1,000 questions for the benchmark
without writing or editing any questions or answers.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Training Data Selection and Matching.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Excluding the 1,000 benchmark items, the remaining QAs form the training pool.
For a fair comparison with ZwZ, for each image, we take the smaller number of available unique questions
between the two sides and sample that many from each side without replacement,
yielding 8,746 image-matched QA pairs.
We then duplicate 254 randomly chosen pairs on both sides to reach 9,000 samples per dataset.
Both training sets thus use identical source images (ZwZ retains its bounding-box overlays)
and differ solely in the questions.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T1" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 1: </span><span id="S4.T1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Comparison with existing fine-grained perception benchmarks.</span>
<em id="S4.T1.10" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">QA authoring</em>: who writes the questions and answers;
Model+Human denotes model-generated questions refined by human annotators,
and Model denotes questions authored entirely by models,
with humans only deciding which candidates to include.
<em id="S4.T1.11" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Blind filter</em>: questions answerable without the image are removed during construction.
<em id="S4.T1.12" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Local verif.</em>: answers are automatically verified on the zoomed evidence region.
<em id="S4.T1.13" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Dual-view</em>: both the full image and the evidence region are provided.
<em id="S4.T1.14" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Dedicated distractor generation</em>: a separate stage for constructing distractor options
(Section <a href="#S3.SS3" title="3.3 Quality Verification and Multi-Source Distractors ‣ 3 ZoomGain Data Construction Pipeline ‣ ZoomGain: Mining Global-to-Zoom Perception Gaps for Fine-Grained Visual Supervision" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.3</span></a>).
In this column, <span id="S4.T1.15" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#666666;">✗</span> indicates that no dedicated stage is reported,
and N/A denotes open-ended evaluation.
“–” denotes not provided or not specified.</figcaption>

<td id="S4.T1.16.1.8.9" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t" style="padding-left:4.5pt;padding-right:4.5pt;"><span id="S4.T1.16.1.8.9.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#00B300;--ltx-bg-color:#F3F0FF;">✓</span></td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
</span></div>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Experiments on ZoomGain Bench</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To examine whether questions mined from global-to-zoom perception gaps
pose a genuine challenge to current VLMs,
we evaluate 28 widely-used VLMs on ZoomGainBench,
spanning closed-source frontier, agentic, fine-grained enhanced single-forward,
and open-source general VLMs (Table <a href="#S5.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ Statistics. ‣ 5 Experiments on ZoomGain Bench ‣ ZoomGain: Mining Global-to-Zoom Perception Gaps for Fine-Grained Visual Supervision" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Statistics.</h4>

<div id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">ZoomGainBench contains 1,000 questions over 941 images:
472 attribute recognition, 94 counting, and 434 OCR questions.
Attribute questions have 4 to 6 answer options; counting and OCR questions are open-ended.
Each question has English and Chinese versions (2,000 evaluation instances in total)
and an automatically obtained evidence region specified by its crop box.
Appendix <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Benchmark Question Categories ‣ ZoomGain: Mining Global-to-Zoom Perception Gaps for Fine-Grained Visual Supervision" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a> shows examples of all three question categories.
Table <a href="#S4.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ Training Data Selection and Matching. ‣ 4 Implementation Details and Data Preparation ‣ ZoomGain: Mining Global-to-Zoom Perception Gaps for Fine-Grained Visual Supervision" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> compares ZoomGainBench with existing benchmarks:
it is the only one that combines fully model-authored QAs, automated verification,
and dedicated distractor construction,
and Section <a href="#S5.SS2" title="5.2 Error analysis ‣ 5 Experiments on ZoomGain Bench ‣ ZoomGain: Mining Global-to-Zoom Perception Gaps for Fine-Grained Visual Supervision" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.2</span></a> shows how these distractors reveal errors shared across models.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.T2" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 2: </span><span id="S5.T2.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Evaluation results on ZoomGainBench.</span>
Scores are reported as percentages for English and Chinese questions.
Each language-specific Overall is weighted by the number of questions in each category.
<span id="S5.T2.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Bold</span> and <span id="S5.T2.7" class="ltx_text ltx_underline">underlined</span> scores indicate the best and second-best results
across all models in each column, respectively.</figcaption>

<td id="S5.T2.8.34.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="padding:0.4pt 4.0pt;">56.97</td>
<td id="S5.T2.8.34.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="--ltx-bg-color:#EDF7ED;padding:0.4pt 4.0pt;"><span id="S5.T2.8.34.5.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#EDF7ED;">53.42</span></td>
<td id="S5.T2.8.34.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="padding:0.4pt 4.0pt;"><span id="S5.T2.8.34.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_underline">52.97</span></td>
<td id="S5.T2.8.34.7" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="padding:0.4pt 4.0pt;"><span id="S5.T2.8.34.7.1" class="ltx_text ltx_underline">67.02</span></td>
<td id="S5.T2.8.34.8" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="padding:0.4pt 4.0pt;">58.45</td>
<td id="S5.T2.8.34.9" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="--ltx-bg-color:#EAF2FF;padding:0.4pt 4.0pt;"><span id="S5.T2.8.34.9.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#EAF2FF;">56.67</span></td>
<td id="S5.T2.8.34.10" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="--ltx-bg-color:#F3F0FF;padding:0.4pt 4.0pt;"><span id="S5.T2.8.34.10.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#F3F0FF;">55.05</span></td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Evaluation protocol.</h4>

<div id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Multiple-choice questions are scored by exact match on the selected option,
and counting questions by exact match on the predicted integer.
OCR questions receive their ANLS score if it is at least <math id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.7" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.7</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.7</annotation></semantics></math>,
and zero otherwise.
Prompts, decoding temperature, and thinking-mode settings
for each model are provided in Appendix <a href="#A6" title="Appendix F ZoomGainBench Evaluation Settings ‣ ZoomGain: Mining Global-to-Zoom Perception Gaps for Fine-Grained Visual Supervision" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.1 </span>Benchmark results.</h3>

<div id="S5.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">ZoomGain challenges even frontier VLMs.</span>
The strongest model, GPT-5.6-Sol, reaches an overall score of only 61.08 (Table <a href="#S5.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ Statistics. ‣ 5 Experiments on ZoomGain Bench ‣ ZoomGain: Mining Global-to-Zoom Perception Gaps for Fine-Grained Visual Supervision" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>), and only five models exceed 50.
All four closed-source models outperform every open-source general VLM:
even GPT-5.5 (56.79) surpasses Qwen3.8-Flash-Next (55.05),
the best open-source general model.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Fine-grained enhanced VLMs are highly competitive.</span>
ZwZ-8B and Vision-OPD-9B improve over their respective base models,
Qwen3-VL-8B and Qwen3.5-9B, by 18.47 and 14.00 points.
Despite its smaller size, ZwZ-8B (47.85) also surpasses Qwen3.5-397B-A17B (45.16).</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Attribute recognition is the most difficult category.</span>
Attribute recognition yields the lowest score averaged over both languages for 23 of 28 models,
despite being the only multiple-choice category, with a uniform-guessing accuracy of about 21.5%.
Qwen3-VL-8B, for example, falls below this level in both languages (15.89 in English and 19.92 in Chinese),
motivating an analysis of which distractors attract incorrect choices.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.2 </span>Error analysis</h3>

<figure id="S5.F3" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2611.14076v1/error_analysis.svg" id="S5.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/211;" width="476" height="211"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 3: </span><span id="S5.F3.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Where models fail on ZoomGain Bench.</span>
(a) How often each model group chooses each type of distractor
compared with the random baseline, considering only incorrect answers.
Values above 1 indicate over-selection.
<em id="S5.F3.5" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Global-view error + blind guess</em> denotes distractors produced both as incorrect answers
when models view the full image and as guesses based on language priors without an image.
(b) How often the 26 models not used in construction
(all evaluated models except Qwen3.5-397B-A17B and Qwen3-VL-235B-A22B-Instruct)
choose global-view errors, grouped by each error’s frequency
in the 30 full-image answers collected during construction.
(c) Accuracy by quartile of the anchor’s area in the full image.</figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Models are misled by global-view errors.</h4>

<div id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Since every distractor retains its source from construction
(Section <a href="#S3.SS3" title="3.3 Quality Verification and Multi-Source Distractors ‣ 3 ZoomGain Data Construction Pipeline ‣ ZoomGain: Mining Global-to-Zoom Perception Gaps for Fine-Grained Visual Supervision" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.3</span></a>),
we can trace where incorrect choices go.
Across all 28 models, global-view-error distractors
receive 71.7% of incorrect choices, exceeding the random baseline of 54.5%,<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
                
                
                
              The baseline assumes that whenever a model answers incorrectly,
it selects uniformly at random among that question’s distractors.</span></span></span>
whereas blind guesses and visual evidence receive only 0.54 and 0.59 times their random-baseline
(Figure <a href="#S5.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 5.2 Error analysis ‣ 5 Experiments on ZoomGain Bench ‣ ZoomGain: Mining Global-to-Zoom Perception Gaps for Fine-Grained Visual Supervision" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>(a)).
This over-selection holds for every model, including those not involved in construction
Moreover, wrong answers that appear more often during construction are also chosen more often by other models.
Among the 26 models not used in construction,
errors that appeared 1–2 times in the 30 full-image answers are chosen 17.7% of the time,
versus 46.0% for those that appeared more than 10 times
(Figure <a href="#S5.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 5.2 Error analysis ‣ 5 Experiments on ZoomGain Bench ‣ ZoomGain: Mining Global-to-Zoom Perception Gaps for Fine-Grained Visual Supervision" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>(b)).
That is, models reproduce the global-view confusions observed during construction,
guessing a scene-plausible answer instead of resolving the queried detail,
such as naming a hockey equipment brand for the logo on a hockey player’s pants
(shown in Figure <a href="#A5.F8" title="Figure 8 ‣ Appendix E Representative Failure Cases ‣ ZoomGain: Mining Global-to-Zoom Perception Gaps for Fine-Grained Visual Supervision" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>(a) in Appendix <a href="#A5" title="Appendix E Representative Failure Cases ‣ ZoomGain: Mining Global-to-Zoom Perception Gaps for Fine-Grained Visual Supervision" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E</span></a>).
<span id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">In other words, distractors mined from global-view errors capture confusions shared across models,
rather than idiosyncrasies of the models used in construction.</span></p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Smaller targets are harder.</h4>

<div id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Accuracy rises with the fraction of the image occupied by the anchor for every model group
(Figure <a href="#S5.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 5.2 Error analysis ‣ 5 Experiments on ZoomGain Bench ‣ ZoomGain: Mining Global-to-Zoom Perception Gaps for Fine-Grained Visual Supervision" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>(c)):
averaged over all models, it increases from 28.9% on the smallest quartile,
where anchors occupy less than 0.4% of the image, to 55.2% on the largest.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Appendix <a href="#A4" title="Appendix D Additional Error Analysis ‣ ZoomGain: Mining Global-to-Zoom Perception Gaps for Fine-Grained Visual Supervision" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D</span></a> further reports the error analysis regarding open-ended questions,
including how incorrect counts differ from the ground truth,
as well as common OCR error patterns.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Experiments on ZoomGain Training Data</h2>

<section id="S6.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">6.1 </span>Main Results</h3>

<section id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Setup.</h4>

<div id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We conduct the experiment on the image-matched ZoomGain and ZwZ sets described in Section <a href="#S4.SS0.SSS0.Px3" title="Training Data Selection and Matching. ‣ 4 Implementation Details and Data Preparation ‣ ZoomGain: Mining Global-to-Zoom Perception Gaps for Fine-Grained Visual Supervision" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>,
each with 9,000 samples.
We select Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.5-9B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Team (2026)</a></cite> as our base models,
applying RL with GRPO <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shao et al. (2024)</a></cite> using each set under identical settings
(batch size 64, 8 rollouts per question; other details are shown in Appendix <a href="#A7" title="Appendix G Training and Evaluation Settings ‣ ZoomGain: Mining Global-to-Zoom Perception Gaps for Fine-Grained Visual Supervision" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">G</span></a>).
We evaluate on four groups of benchmarks.
<em id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Held-in</em>: ZoomGain Bench.
<em id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Held-out fine-grained perception</em>: ZoomBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wei et al. (2026)</a></cite>, V* Bench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu and Xie (2023)</a></cite>,
HR-Bench 4K and 8K <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al. (2025b)</a></cite>, MME-RealWorld-Lite <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al. (2024)</a></cite>,
TreeBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al. (2025a)</a></cite>, and VisualProbe <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lai et al. (2025)</a></cite>.
<em id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">General perception</em>: CV-Bench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tong et al. (2024a)</a></cite>, MMStar <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al. (2024)</a></cite>, and MMVP <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tong et al. (2024b)</a></cite>.
<em id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Difficult perception and reasoning</em>: BabyVision <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al. (2026)</a></cite>,
PerceptionBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lin et al. (2026)</a></cite>,
and O3-Bench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al. (2026a)</a></cite>.
We also compare with some large parameter VLMs, including open-source and closed-source  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Google DeepMind (2025)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">OpenAI ()</a></cite>.
We report the average score over the 13 held-out benchmarks, excluding ZoomGain Bench.
Because ZoomGain Bench and the ZoomGain training data are generated by the same generation pipeline,
including it could favor ZoomGain model.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S6.T3" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 3: </span><span id="S6.T3.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Results of RL training on ZoomGain and ZwZ data.</span>

over the ZwZ-trained and base models, respectively;

<td id="S6.T3.6.1.20.9" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_l ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_r" style="padding:0.6pt 1.5pt;"><span id="S6.T3.6.1.20.9.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#16A34A;--ltx-bg-color:#EFEFEF;">+11.65</span></td>

<td id="S6.T3.6.1.20.15" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_l ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_r" style="padding:0.6pt 1.5pt;"><span id="S6.T3.6.1.20.15.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#16A34A;--ltx-bg-color:#EFEFEF;">+11.60</span></td>
<td id="S6.T3.6.1.20.16" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_l ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="padding:0.6pt 1.5pt;"><span id="S6.T3.6.1.20.16.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#16A34A;--ltx-bg-color:#EFEFEF;">+6.35</span></td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
</span></div>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Results.</h4>

<div id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As shown in Table <a href="#S6.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ Setup. ‣ 6.1 Main Results ‣ 6 Experiments on ZoomGain Training Data ‣ ZoomGain: Mining Global-to-Zoom Perception Gaps for Fine-Grained Visual Supervision" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>,
models trained on ZoomGain data consistently outperform their ZwZ-trained counterparts on all 14 benchmarks.
Since the two training sets differ solely in the questions,
these gains can be attributed to the questions constructed by ZoomGain.
Moreover, the improvements brought by ZoomGain extend across all benchmark groups.
Compared with the base models, the gains of ZwZ are mainly concentrated on fine-grained perception.
In contrast, ZoomGain improves all three groups.
The advantage of ZoomGain over ZwZ is most pronounced on difficult perception and reasoning,
where the 9B model gains 11.01 points on O3-Bench and the 4B model gains 10.31 points on BabyVision.
These results indicate that ZoomGain data
enables models to acquire transferable fine-grained perception capabilities.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Remarkably, with only 9K training samples,
the 9B model achieves an average score of 66.10,
surpassing Qwen3.5-397B-A17B (65.55) and performing on par with GLM-5.3-Flash (66.07),
while the 4B model (63.96) also surpasses Qwen3.5-122B-A10B and the ZwZ-trained 9B model.
Moreover, ZoomGain-trained models achieve the best results among all compared models on 6 of 7 fine-grained perception benchmarks.
However, we also notice that the strongest large models still lead on
general perception and difficult perception and reasoning,
suggesting that these tasks still rely heavily on model scale and reasoning capability.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">6.2 </span>Ablation Study</h3>

<section id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Setup.</h4>

<div id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We ablate two core designs of ZoomGain on Qwen3.5-4B.
All variants use 9K training samples,
with the same RL settings and evaluation protocol
as in Table <a href="#S6.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ Setup. ‣ 6.1 Main Results ‣ 6 Experiments on ZoomGain Training Data ‣ ZoomGain: Mining Global-to-Zoom Perception Gaps for Fine-Grained Visual Supervision" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>.
<span id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(1)</span> Remove incremental evidence:
instead of requiring questions to be based on incremental information
that appears only in the zoomed-view caption,
we generate questions directly from the zoomed-view caption.
The source images, candidate QA pool size, and 9K sample selection procedure
are otherwise identical to those of the full version.
<span id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(2)</span> Remove dedicated distractors:
we keep each question, its answer, the correct option’s position,
and the number of options unchanged,
and replace only the distractors of each multiple-choice question
with correct answers from other training questions in the same answer category
(e.g., color or material).
OCR and counting questions are open-ended and are unaffected by this ablation.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S6.T4" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 4: </span><span id="S6.T4.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Ablation of incremental evidence and dedicated distractors.</span> Avg. is computed over the 10 held-out benchmarks.</figcaption>

</span></div>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Results.</h4>

<div id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As shown in Table <a href="#S6.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ Setup. ‣ 6.2 Ablation Study ‣ 6 Experiments on ZoomGain Training Data ‣ ZoomGain: Mining Global-to-Zoom Perception Gaps for Fine-Grained Visual Supervision" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, the results demonstrate that both designs contribute to training performance.
The full ZoomGain pipeline achieves the highest average score across the 10 held-out benchmarks.
Removing any component incude the performance losses on almost all benchmarks. Both ablations incur the largest losses in the
<span id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">difficult perception and reasoning</span> group.
The full version improves over the base model by an average of 6.19 points
across these three benchmarks,
while each ablation retains only about half of this gain.
This indicates that the two designs mainly improve the capability of perception
and reasoning that transfer beyond the training distribution.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The effect of incremental evidence is most apparent on fine-grained benchmarks:
removing it reduces scores on ZoomBench and VisualProbe by 3.43 and 4.46 points, respectively.
This indicates that restricting questions to evidence revealed only after zooming
forces the model to learn to locate and recognize details hard to discern.
Meanwhile, removing dedicated distractors causes the largest drop
on the held-in ZoomGainBench, at 8.96 points.
It is expected because the benchmark’s options are constructed using the same pipeline.
Using dedicated distractors introduces harder confusions,
forcing the model to attend more closely to visual details and thereby enhancing its perception capabilities under the same data budget.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S7" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">7 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S7.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To address the difficulty of constructing reliable fine-grained visual supervision at scale,
we propose ZoomGain, a data construction pipeline that exploits the perception gap
between global and zoomed-in views.
ZoomGain turns details revealed only by zooming into questions about the full image,
verifies their answers on the zoomed view with multiple models,
and mines multi-source distractors that could mislead VLMs.
With this pipeline, we construct ZoomGainBench, a challenging benchmark
whose questions and answers are entirely model-authored. Through the analysis of failure cases, we find that different VLMs share similar confusions
when fine details are unresolved in the full image.
Experiments further show the effectiveness of ZoomGain data as training supervision,
which consistently improves VLMs’ capabilities of fine-grained perception,
general perception, and difficult perception and reasoning.</p>
</div>
</section>
